BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: A short lived high pressure system will continue to build in over the region Sunday, bringing slightly warmer temperatures and dry conditions through Monday morning.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread precipitation through Friday morning, along with isolated to scattered thunderstorms.
- Thunderstorms through this evening will be capable of producing gusty winds and brief heavy rain, and small hail in Southwest Idaho.
- Windy conditions will develop late tonight and tomorrow behind a cold front, with much cooler conditions Friday and Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: An area of showers and thunderstorms has developed across SW Idaho this afternoon, extending from the OR/ID border into s-central Idaho. The mid-level feature triggering this activity will continue northward through this evening, extending the coverage of showers/storms along its path. The showers/storms will bring gusty winds and moderate rainfall. While the severe wind threat has diminished some, stronger thunderstorms will be capable of wind gusts to 50 mph and brief heavy rain through early evening. Showers continue overnight, with a 10-15% chance of thunderstorms over portions of SW Idaho (mainly the w-central ID mtns). While the wind threat diminishes this evening, brief heavy rain will still be possible from storms overnight and the threat for flooding or debris flows on burns scars remains a risk.

The surface cold front will cross the area later tonight, arriving with gusty northwest winds. Widespread gusts of 30 to 40 mph, will develop across SE Oregon and SW Idaho from the Snake Plain to the NV border. Local gusts of 45 to 55 mph will impact windier locations of Baker and northern Malheur counties through sunrise Friday. The upper low lifts to the northeast on Friday with precipitation tapering off from W-E during the afternoon. Post frontal northwest winds will remain gusty with speeds of 30-40 mph through evening. Snow levels will drop to between 4500-6000 feet over Oregon and between 6-8kft over SW Idaho as precipitations wraps up on Friday. Minor accumulations are possible over higher peaks.
Saturday will see dry and cool conditions with breezy northwest winds. It could start off frosty at lower elevations, though the breezy winds could keep it localized.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A short lived high pressure system will continue to build in over the region Sunday, bringing slightly warmer temperatures and dry conditions through Monday morning. Clear skies overnight paired with the recent precipitation will allow for valley fog to form late Sunday night and again on Monday night, but it should dissipate by the late morning. A cut off low pressure system from the Gulf of Alaska will move in late Monday-early Tuesday, bringing widespread precipitation and cooler temperatures to the region. Disagreement in the timing of the low pressure system exists, with most models pushing precipitation and cooler temperatures late Monday, while a few outlier solutions delay the arrival to Tuesday morning. Current forecast favors high terrain in northeast Oregon and central Idaho for the best chance of precipitation (30-50% chance) through Thursday, with snow levels anticipated to be around 6000-7000 feet. The low will then push to the east, allowing for another ridge of high pressure to build in by Thursday, bringing another slight warming and drying trend for the region.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Into the long term our temperatures will drop several degrees below average under a colder airmass with some increasing chances for precipitation, primarily for our eastern zones this time, with temperatures then warming to near average by the middle of the work week under brief clearing.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above average temperatures will continue through the end of the week, but a weekend system will drop temperatures towards near to below average.
- Precipitation is possible this afternoon through Sunday, with the potential for frozen precipitation outside of the mountains Sunday morning.
- Near normal temperatures and a bit warmer by Tuesday into Wednesday, but next Pacific system will be approaching from the Pacific Northwest by the middle of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Short term forecast remains seasonably warm with above average temperatures but accompanying this will be chances of precipitation. At the upper levels, a deep low is moving inland across California and will continue to lift northeast through Friday. Unfortunately for our precipitation chances, this system will see it's energy split into two segments - the initial cutoff low will become absorbed into troughing to the north in Central Canada and merge with this feature, while the remnant energy will continue eastwards and form a new cutoff low that will be approaching the Four Corners region by Saturday morning. This means our forecast area will sit in a split flow that will not favor increased moisture, but we could see some gusty winds alongside areas of showers today with Friday a bit drier.

For this afternoon and tonight, a plume of moisture lifting up across the region with PWAT values in the 0.6-1.0 inch range alongside some meager forcing including orographic lift will produce areas of showers across the high terrain of our western zones, primarily Carbon and Albany Counties. Some of this activity may be able to make it off of the high terrain and down into the lower elevations including portions of Platte and Laramie Counties, but should struggle to survive much further east than this thanks to increasing stability despite much higher moisture values. Also of note, very weak instability is expected across this area, which may allow for some thunder but not much more.

Overnight and into tomorrow morning widespread cloud cover will insulate the region and prevent lows from dropping any further than the mid 40's to mid to upper 50's. While this shouldn't bring record warm low temperatures, this will be around 20 degrees above normal for this time of year, allowing for a relatively muggy start to Friday morning. We'll see this moisture clear out however as a dry slot overspreads and mostly removes our precipitation chances for the day. The one exception to this will be late Friday into Saturday morning along and ahead of a cold front that will be moving across the region ahead of the stronger system lifting into Canada. Enough forcing won't be present until this feature is already halfway through our region, but expect a chance at some scattered showers across extreme southeastern Wyoming and through the Nebraska Panhandle. This dry air on Friday will also drop our minimum daytime RH values back into the 20-30% range east of the Laramie Range, and while not critical, this will bring an elevated risk of Fire Weather conditions alongside the other story for the day - strong winds. While the split in flow will somehow avoid the CWA almost fully, with a 700mb jet max both to our east and northwest, elevated winds will be likely during the morning and afternoon for our western and northern zones, with another quick fork of the jet grazing our region around midnight and increasing winds from the I-25 corridor eastwards through the nighttime hours. The strength of this feature won't be enough to promote wind highlights for the region, but should bring some gusty conditions for the time period. The aforementioned cold front will then begin to drop our temperatures, with overnight lows in the 30's to 40's as we move into the weekend where temperatures will become below average.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Into the long term our temperatures will drop several degrees below average under a colder airmass with some increasing chances for precipitation, primarily for our eastern zones this time, with temperatures then warming to near average by the middle of the work week under brief clearing. The upper level pattern will see the northern trough quickly accelerating eastwards, leaving us under southwesterly flow aloft from a brief finger of weak transient ridging that will quickly be erased by low pressure slowly progressing across the Four Corners region. This will then become our main weather feature through Monday before finally sliding eastwards into the Central Plains, with another transient ridge building on Tuesday that will briefly hold the region before another Pacific low moves into the Pacific Northwest and then starts to knock on our doorstep by Wednesday into Thursday. Under this pattern, we should see surface flow begin to weaken by later Saturday and continue into the early part of next week as the strongest part of the jet remains just south and west of the forecast area. With this flow, the best moisture will remain just outside of our forecast area to the east as well. That being said, PWAT values will still be on the higher side even for our area by around 0.15-0.25 inch, and scattered shower activity is expected from Saturday afternoon and continuing through Monday evening before exiting the region. The highest QPF amounts should align with the best moisture for the southeastern portions of the Nebraska Panhandle, but some meager moisture should occur across most of the forecast area east of the Laramie Range. Morning lows both Sunday and Monday could also allow for this to mix with snow, but don't expect noteworthy winter accumulations at this time. As conditions finally clear later Monday into Tuesday and the transient ridge moves in, 700mb temperatures will warm back into the 5-8 C range, allowing surface temperatures to rise back to near average in the 50-60 degree range. Tightening pressure gradients from the approaching Pacific system will start to increase westerly to southwesterly winds again for our western zones on Tuesday and Wednesday, but otherwise expect conditions to be a bit more uneventful as precipitation chances dwindle outside of the high terrain for the middle of the week.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: As we move towards next week, models are also in fairly good agreement that dry zonal flow will begin to propagate the region by Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread rain continues through early Friday.
- Flooding/Flash Flooding is likely across portions of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah.
- Modeled responses suggest several rivers reaching bankfull or higher at river forecast points across southwest Colorado and southeast Utah.
- Strong to severe thunderstorms will be possible today, favoring the Four Corners area. That threat begins to gradually diminish overnight.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Southwesterly flow continues to dominate the region, which is working to continuously advect subtropical moisture into western Colorado and eastern Utah this afternoon. Certain locations in southwest Colorado and southeast Utah are already overperforming the forecast, which means the risk of flash flooding/flooding is ongoing in some areas, if not likely to occur. Please continue to stay weather aware in the coming hours. Additionally, there is a threat for embedded thunderstorms within these rain showers, particularly in the Four Corners area this afternoon. Some storms are capable of producing small hail, gusty winds, and additional heavy rainfall. As we approach sunset, the threat for convective activity gradually diminishes and showers appear to shift to more stratiform in nature. Precipitation chances will continue into the overnight hours before scattering out by Friday afternoon. Shower and thunderstorm chances don't stay away for long as Friday night into Saturday morning will see additional shower and storm activity, particularly south of the I-70 corridor. This is mainly due to residual moisture from the previous system in combination with a new low pressure system forecast to track over the region this weekend.

Models stay in fairly good agreement through the weekend that unsettled weather will remain in the forecast. The timing and specific track of the next low pressure system is still uncertain, therefore there are still unknowns. All in all, precipitation chances remain in the forecast this weekend.

As we move towards next week, models are also in fairly good agreement that dry zonal flow will begin to propagate the region by Monday. Because of this, we will be seeing cooler than normal temperatures, with the potential for overnight lows to drop below freezing for a couple hours at a time. Keep in mind, this is still far out, so confidence remains low on this matter.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Monday through Wednesday...Residual isolated showers are possible Monday from the outgoing weekend system. Late Monday, the low will move out of CO into NE, taking the moisture in the area with it.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flood Watch remains through the day Friday for the eastern San Juan mountains and the Upper Rio Grande Valley, with areal stream/river flooding and rock/mud slides possible.
- Periods of moderate to heavy rain for the Continental Divide, tonight into early Friday, with strong to severe storms possible across the southern tier.
- Cooler and wetter weather area wide this weekend, with gradual warming and drying early next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Current water vapor imagery and upper air analysis has moderate southwest aloft across the region, with upper level ridging translating the Southern and Central High Plains, as a deep upper trough continues to dig across the West Coast. Water vapor imagery is also indicating several embedded short waves lifting out across the Desert Southwest and Great Basin at this time, with GOES Total Blended Precipitable Water imagery indicating ample sup- tropical moisture (PWATs 200-250 percent of normal) embedded within the flow across Desert Southwest through the Southern and Central Rockies at this time.

Latest model data supports increasing southwest flow aloft across the region through the day Friday, as embedded short waves lift out ahead of the West Coast upper trough lifting out across the Intermountain West and Great Basin overnight. This supports one round of showers and embedded thunderstorms, lifting out across the region this afternoon and evening, with another round associated with the translating system across the Great Basin later this evening into early Friday morning. With the ample moisture in place, moderate to heavy rainfall remains the main concern, especially across the eastern San Juan Mtns into the San Luis Valley, where 1 to 2 inches of precipitation has already fallen, with another 1 to 2 inches possible by early Friday morning. Along with the heavy rain threat, there remains the potential for a few strong to severe storms across the southern tier tonight, the ample moisture supporting CAPE of 500-1000 j/kg combined with increasing shear of 40-60 kts. The main threat from these stronger storms would be strong winds up to 60 mph and hail up to an inch in diameter, with an isolated tornado not out of the question, as latest cams continuing to indicate some updraft helicity swaths lifting out across the Southwest Mtns into the San Luis Valley.

For Friday, strong west to southwest flow continues aloft, as the main upper system continues to lift out across the Northern Rockies, with models continuing to indicate secondary energy digging across the Great Basin and developing another closed upper low across the Desert Southwest by Friday night. This supports breezy southwest winds across the higher terrain through the day, with gusty south to southwest winds of 20 to 40 mph mixing across the lower elevations Friday morning and afternoon. Precipitation winds down across the area through the morning hours, with scattered showers and thunderstorms expected to develop once again, especially across the Southern Mtns into the Southeast Plains Friday afternoon and evening. With strong shear remaining in place, some of these storms could be strong to marginally severe once again, with hail and strong winds being the main threats. Temperatures warm into the 70s to low 80s across the plains, with highs mainly in the 50s and 60s across the higher terrain, save for 40s at the peaks.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Saturday into Sunday...The southern low from the aforementioned split will begin to deepen over AZ and help moisture return to CO. This moisture along with WAA and good synoptic forcing will support more widespread precipitation across the region. Light to moderate rain is expected, but a locally heavy shower cannot be ruled out. WPC's Day 3 (Sat) Excessive Rain Outlook includes parts of SE CO in the SLGT risk area and was updated to include western CO in a MRGL risk earlier today. Day 4 (Sun) also has part of the region in a SLGT risk, but a much smaller area in far SE CO. There is the potential for flash flooding in areas which experience locally higher rainfall totals for both Saturday and Sunday. QPFs of 1.5-2 inches are expected across SE CO over the weekend, with locally higher totals possible. Given this system's pattern of producing severe weather across the Desert Southwest, it is not out of the realm of possibility for a low end severe threat to exist on Saturday. This will depend on the position of the instability axis, its strength, and its northern extent. The northern low will help push a cold front into CO on Saturday faster and further south than previous guidance showed. High temperatures will drop into the 50s and 60s across the high valleys and plains. With colder temperatures, snow levels will drop to 9,500ft. It is possible that a few inches of snow could accumulate on terrain above 10,000ft. These colder temps will persist through the weekend and into Monday.

Monday through Wednesday...Residual isolated showers are possible Monday from the outgoing weekend system. Late Monday, the low will move out of CO into NE, taking the moisture in the area with it. Broad upper level ridging will develop over the region for Tuesday and Wednesday. Gradual warming begins Tuesday, with generally dry and more seasonably type temperatures in place by midweek.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: As the initial low ejects into the northern Rockies, a secondary upper low is forecast to form over the Desert Southwest Saturday, then slowly translate into the central/southern Rockies Sunday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Numerous Flood and Flash Flood Warnings remain in effect for southern and eastern Utah, as widespread moderate to heavy precipitation persists through this evening.
- There is a Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) for severe thunderstorms much of Utah through this evening, with a threat for large hail and damaging winds.

- Accumulating snowfall is expected across the higher terrain of northern Utah tonight into Friday morning, with 1-4" likely above 9000 feet. There is a chance of locally higher amounts for favored locations.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Tropical moisture in place across the forecast area will continue to fuel widespread showers and thunderstorms through this evening, as an upstream low along the California coast makes its way through the Great Basin. Ample deep layer shear will maintain a favorable environment for organized convection including supercells anywhere sufficient breaks in the cloud cover allow for destabilization, as has been evidenced across southwest Utah over the past few hours. Efficient rainfall rates will also continue to result in excessive runoff. Most large drainages across south central into east central Utah are already running high and fast, and as such Flood Warnings are in effect for these areas.

A shortwave trough rounding the base of the upstream low will lift across the forecast area this evening, focusing the heavier precipitation further north into northern Utah/southwest Wyoming. Initially a band of showers and thunderstorms, potentially strong to severe, is expected to propagate across northwest Utah reaching the Wasatch Front this evening, followed by a fairly broad stratiform region of precipitation associated with the passage of the upper trough. Snow levels will fall to roughly 8000 feet overnight, with accumulating snow largely above 9000 feet. Previous forecast totals of 1-4" with locally higher amounts still look reasonable, with a few locally higher totals if precip is able to linger into Friday morning.

As the initial low ejects into the northern Rockies, a secondary upper low is forecast to form over the Desert Southwest Saturday, then slowly translate into the central/southern Rockies Sunday. This will maintain cool temperatures across the forecast area, along with a chance of precipitation mainly across the eastern third of the CWA. An upper trough across the Pacific Northwest looks to keep temperatures near to slightly below climo for much of next week.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Andrew McWilliams
bottom_line: A moisture-laden storm arrives in Colorado on Wednesday, bringing early-season avalanche concerns to steep, snow-covered slopes. Nearly every fall, small avalanches catch eager snow riders, late-season hikers, and hunters off guard. If you are traveling through the high country over the next few days, exercise caution on steep, snow-covered terrain.

For Wednesday and Thursday, in areas with snow already on the ground, rain falling on the early snowpack increases the potential for Wet Loose avalanches. From Thursday through the weekend, as new snow accumulates and wind-drifted snow obscures the ground cover, dry slab and loose avalanches will become a threat at the highest elevations. It doesn't take much snow on steep grassy slopes, rock slabs, or remnant snowfields for slides to occur.
We will update the Statewide Avalanche Conditions as necessary. On November 1, 2026, we will resume our daily weather and avalanche forecasts.
We will update the Field Report and Avalanche Observations as information comes in, so please send us your observations.
An impressive tropical moisture stream takes aim at the Southern Mountains this week.

Wednesday & Thursday: During the early parts of the storm, precipitation will start as rain. Under specific storm cells dropping high-intensity precipitation and at the highest elevations, you can expect a few inches of snow by Thursday morning.

Thursday Night & Friday: A cold front will drop temperatures and snow levels. Expect 6 to 12+ inches of snow above treeline in the San Juan Mountains by Friday morning. The Central Mountains may see several inches in favored areas, with lighter accumulation further north.

Saturday through Monday: A closed low-pressure system crosses the Four Corners region, bringing additional snow. Depending on the storm's exact track, the Southern Mountains could see over 6 additional inches, while the Central and Northern Mountains can expect up to 6 inches.
The storm moves east on Tuesday, bringing a short-lived high-pressure ridge before another potential storm arrives for Halloween weekend.

You can get up-to-date point weather forecasts on our Weather Forecasts page by clicking on the map or searching for a location. You can also get model forecasts on our Point Forecasts page and Model Forecast page. You can check current weather conditions across Colorado on our Weather Stations page.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
